saint.name: St. Sergius of Radonezh
saint.summary: As a boy, Saint Sergius could not learn to read. He prayed in tears over his letters until a stranger under an oak gave him a piece of holy bread that tasted like honey. As a young man he wanted only to be alone with God, in a forest far from any road. For a while he had it, with wolves coming by his hut and a bear that waited for its bread like a creditor. Then monks came through the trees and begged to stay. What does a man do when God answers his prayer for solitude with a crowd? Saint Sergius of Radonezh spent his life finding out.
saint.biography:
For a long time Saint Sergius asked God for one thing: to live without a single person near him. In a forest near Radonezh, God gave it to him. He had a hut and a small wooden church. No road led there, no village stood nearby, and wolves came by night and by day. Today that place is the Trinity Lavra, the great shrine of the Russian Church. The Church calls the man who wanted to be alone there the abbot of all Russia, the Hegumen of the Russian land.1

He founded the monastery that grew into the Lavra, and at the Patriarch’s word he gave it the common life, in which no monk owns anything. His disciples carried that life to new monasteries. He turned down the highest seat in the Russian Church. Before the war with Mamai, he blessed the Grand Prince of Moscow. He had asked for none of it. The story begins with a boy who could not read.2

A Boy Who Cannot Read Meets a Stranger

Saint Sergius was born Bartholomew, in the land of Rostov. His father was Saint Kirill and his mother was Saint Maria. They belonged to the boyars, the nobles of Rostov. Before the boy was born, he cried out three times from his mother’s womb during one Sunday Liturgy. The women around her wondered what this child would be. As a baby he would not take milk on Wednesdays and Fridays, the fast days of the week.3

At seven he was sent to learn his letters. His brothers Stefan and Petr learned quickly, but Saint Sergius could not. His teacher punished him, his parents scolded him, and his schoolmates reproached him. So he went off alone and prayed with tears, asking the Lord to teach him and give him understanding.4

One day his father sent him out to look for some foals. In a field he came upon an old monk in a black robe, standing under an oak and praying with tears. The boy bowed, came near, and waited until the prayer was done. Then the old man looked at him and called him over. He blessed the boy and kissed him, and asked what he was looking for. The boy had been sent for foals, but he asked for something else.5

“Holy father, pray to God for me, so that I can learn to read.”6

The old man lifted his hands and prayed, and he said “Amen.” Then he reached into his pocket, and with three fingers he took out a small piece of white wheat bread. It was holy bread, blessed at the Liturgy, and he held it out like a treasure. “Open your mouth, child. Take this and eat.” The bread tasted as sweet as honey. The boy remembered the psalm that calls God’s words sweeter than honey, and he said it aloud. Then the old man told him not to grieve over his letters any longer. He said that from that day the Lord would give him better knowledge than his brothers and friends had.7

The boy fell at his feet in tears. He begged the stranger to come home with him, because his parents loved such men very much. Saint Kirill and Saint Maria came out and bowed to their guest. A meal was ready. But the old man went first into the family chapel and took the boy with him. He began the set prayers and told the boy to read a psalm. “I cannot,” the boy said. The old man told him to read without doubting. So Saint Sergius read, and he read clearly and well. His parents and brothers stood amazed, and they praised God.8

At the table the parents begged their guest to stay. They told him about the three cries before the child was born, and they asked him to ease their worry about the boy. He told them not to be afraid. The boy would read well, he said, and he would be great before God and before people. As he was leaving, he spoke the words the family kept.9

“Your son will be a dwelling of the Holy Trinity, and he will lead many after him to understand the commandments of God.”

— The stranger under the oak, in the Life of Sergius

They walked him to the gate, and there he vanished from their sight. Saint Kirill and Saint Maria believed he was an angel, sent to give their son the knowledge of letters.10

From then on the boy could read any book. Before he was twelve he lived on bread and water, and on Wednesdays and Fridays he ate nothing at all. His mother begged him to stop. He answered that no one is clean before God, and he quoted Job and the psalm of David’s repentance. “You are not twelve years old,” she said, “and you speak of your sins.”11

In those years Saint Kirill was still a rich man.

Two Brothers Build a Church in the Forest

Little by little, Saint Kirill lost his wealth. He went often with his prince to the Tatar Horde, and the Horde took heavy tribute. Tatar raids came, and the harvests failed. Worst of all was one great raid. After it, Rostov passed under the power of Moscow. Moscow sent its governors, and they beat the people of Rostov and took their goods. They even hung the eldest boyar of the town upside down, and fear spread through the whole country around. So Saint Kirill gathered his household and moved to Radonezh, a village that the Grand Prince had given to his younger son. Many others from Rostov went with him. The family settled near the church of the Nativity of Christ.12

Stefan and Petr married, but Saint Sergius would not. He wanted the monk’s life with his whole soul, and he asked his father again and again to let him go. “My lord, let me go now, as you promised, so that I can begin the monk’s life with your blessing.” His parents asked him to wait. “We are old, poor, and sick, and there is no one to care for us,” they said. “When you lay us in the grave and cover us with earth, then you will do what you desire.”13

He promised gladly, and he kept his promise. He cared for them every day until both of them took monastic vows, each in a monastery of their own. A few years later they died, and to their last breath they blessed him. He sang the funeral hymns over them, kissed them, and laid them in the grave with tears. For forty days he kept their memory with prayers and services, and with alms and food for the poor. Then he went home with a glad heart, as if he had found a treasure. Now nothing held him back.14

He looked at the house and everything in it, and he wanted none of it. He remembered the psalm of David: “I would go far away and stay in the wilderness, hoping in God, who saves me.” What he wanted more than anything was the monk’s life, lived “in fasting and silence.” So he called his younger brother Petr and gave him the whole inheritance, and he kept nothing for himself.15

Their older brother Stefan was a monk by then. He had lived only a short time with his wife before she died, leaving him two sons, one of them named Ivan. Then he had entered the monastery of the Intercession at Khotkovo. Saint Sergius went to him there and asked him to come along and look for a lonely place. Stefan agreed and left the monastery. The two brothers walked through many forests until they came to a place deep in the thicket where there was a spring of water. They walked around it and came to love it, and they prayed.16

With their own hands they cut down trees and carried the logs on their shoulders. First they built a roofed hut to sleep in, with a storeroom. Then they built a cell, and then a small church. When it stood ready, Saint Sergius asked his older brother which saint or feast the church should honor. “You know the answer to your question as well as I do,” said Stefan. Their parents had often told Saint Sergius, “You are a gift of God and not our son.” Priests had explained the three cries before his birth: the boy would be a disciple of the Holy Trinity. So the church must bear the name of the Holy Trinity.17

Saint Sergius sighed from the depth of his heart. “You have spoken rightly, my lord.” He had wanted the same thing all along, he said, and he had asked only out of humility. Priests came from Saint Theognostus, the Metropolitan who led the Russian Church. They brought what was needed for the altar, with holy relics of martyrs. They consecrated the church to the Holy Trinity, early in the reign of Grand Prince Simeon of Moscow.18

Stefan stayed a while longer. Then he saw how hard the life was. There was no food and nothing to drink, and nothing could be brought in. There was no road and no path, no village and no house, and no one ever passed by. On every side stood the forest. Stefan grew weary of it. He left the wilderness and his own brother and went to Moscow, to the Epiphany monastery. There he lived a strict life and sang in the choir beside Saint Alexis, a monk who would one day be Metropolitan. Grand Prince Simeon later made Stefan abbot of that monastery and took him as his own spiritual father.19

The two were brothers of one father and one mother, and they had chosen the place together. One of them wanted a monastery in the city. The other “made the wilderness like a city.”20

Saint Sergius had his solitude now, and he was not yet even a monk.

Saint Sergius Becomes a Monk and Lives Alone

He would not take the monk’s robe until he had learned the whole rule of monastic life. Then he invited an abbot named Mitrofan to his hermitage in the forest. He bowed at Mitrofan’s feet and asked him again and again to make him a monk. He had wanted it since his youth, he said, and only his parents’ will had held him back.21

“Now I am free of everything, and I thirst to be made a monk. As a deer longs for a spring of water, so my soul thirsts for a monk’s life in the wilderness.”

— Saint Sergius to the abbot Mitrofan, in the Life of Sergius

Mitrofan made him a monk in that church on 7 October, the feast of the martyrs Saint Sergius and Saint Bacchus. So the new monk took the name Sergius. He was twenty-three years old. When he received Holy Communion, a sweet fragrance filled the church and was felt outside it too. For seven days he stayed in the church and ate nothing but the holy bread from the abbot’s hand. The psalms were always on his lips: “One day in your courts is better than a thousand.”22

When Mitrofan was ready to go, Saint Sergius saw him off. “Today you are going away, father, and leaving me alone, as I wanted,” he said. “For a long time I have longed with all my thoughts and desires to live alone in the wilderness, without a single person.” God had heard him, he said, and he thanked God for it. Then he asked Mitrofan to teach him how to live alone, how to pray, and how to stand against the enemy, because he had no experience. Mitrofan was amazed that he should ask. He answered with the words of Saint Paul: God is faithful, and He will not let you be tempted beyond your strength. Then he gave Saint Sergius into God’s hands and left him.23

Wild animals came to him often, by night and by day. Wolves came in packs, howling and roaring, and sometimes bears came. Saint Sergius “feared them a little, like any man,” but he turned to God in prayer, and none of them harmed him.24

One night he went into the church to sing the night service. As he began, the wall of the church opened. The devil came in with a crowd of demon warriors, not through the door but like a thief. They wore Lithuanian clothes and tall, pointed Lithuanian caps. They rushed at him as if to tear the church down to the ground, grinding their teeth and threatening to kill him. “Run, go away from here, and do not stay in this place any longer.”25

Saint Sergius armed himself with prayer. He called on the Holy Trinity and put his hope in the Mother of God, whom the Orthodox Church calls the Theotokos, the one who gave birth to God. The Cross was his weapon, and he said the psalm: “Let God rise, and let His enemies vanish.” At once the devil and his army vanished, and Saint Sergius thanked God.26

A few days later they came again. He was praying through the night in his hut, awake and not dreaming, when a noise and a crashing began. A crowd of demons shouted at him to leave. The place was far from people, they said, and he would die of hunger, or robbers or wild beasts would kill him. Before long the power of God covered him and scattered them. He thanked the Lord for not leaving him and for hearing him so quickly. The devil fought so hard because he feared that a monastery would rise in that place.27

Other wild animals came close, circled him, and sniffed at him. One bear began to come often, and Saint Sergius saw that it came for a little food and meant no harm. So he would bring a small piece of bread out of his hut and lay it on a stump or a log. The bear would take the bread in its mouth and go. When there was no bread, it did not go. It stood there a long time and looked around, “like a hard creditor who wants his debt.”28

Saint Sergius had only bread and water from the spring, and not much of either. Often there was no bread for a whole day, and then both he and the bear went hungry. If he had one piece, he broke it in two and gave half to the bear. Sometimes he gave the bear the whole piece and fasted himself, because he would rather go hungry than cheat the animal. The bear came many times a day, and this went on for more than a year.29

No one knew how he lived; only God saw it. He spent whole nights in prayer, and he spoke with God alone. He had tasted the sweetness of silence, and he did not want to give it up.30

About two years went by in this way. Then God put it into the hearts of some monks to come to him through the forest.31

Monks Come and the Bread Runs Out

They came one at a time, then in twos and sometimes in threes. They fell at his feet. “Father, accept us,” they said. “We want to live with you in this place and save our souls.” He would not accept them. “You cannot live in this place,” he told them, “or bear the hardships of the wilderness: hunger, thirst, sorrow, discomfort, poverty, and need.” They said they would bear it with God’s help. “Only do not send us away from you and from this place that we love.”32

He saw their faith, and he gave way.

“I wanted to live alone in this wilderness, brothers, and to die here. But if God has willed it, and if it pleases Him that there be a monastery in this place and many brothers gathered here, let the Lord’s will be done! I receive you with joy…”

— Saint Sergius to the first monks, in the Life of Sergius

He told them to prepare their hearts for patience and many troubles, not for food, drink, or rest. Each man built his own cell. Saint Sergius was young and had the strength of two men, and he served them all like a servant bought with money. He chopped their wood and carried it to each cell. He ground the grain and baked the bread, and he cut and sewed their shoes and clothes. From the spring he carried water up the hill to each brother’s door, in two buckets on his shoulders.33

After a year the abbot Mitrofan, who had made him a monk, fell ill and died. Saint Sergius grieved for him greatly and prayed that God would give the brothers an abbot. The brothers came to him together. “Father, we cannot live without an abbot,” they said, and they asked him to take the place. He sighed from the depth of his soul. “I have never even thought of being abbot. My soul wants one thing: to die a monk in this place.” They told him he must become abbot or find them one, or they would all leave. So in the end he went to the bishop, who made him a priest and the abbot of the little community.34

When he came home, the brothers bowed to the ground. He lay face down in the church and prayed with tears before the icon of the Holy Trinity. Then he turned to them. “Pray for me, brothers, for I am a man of little learning and no experience,” he said. He had been given the care of their souls, and he would have to answer for it.35

For two or three years there were twelve brothers, and Saint Sergius was the thirteenth. He served the Liturgy every day, and he baked the holy bread for it himself. He would let no one else do it, though many wished to. Then one day Stefan came back from Moscow with his younger son Ivan. Holding the boy by the right hand, he led him into the church and gave him to his brother to be made a monk. Saint Sergius gave the boy the name Theodore. The old monks marveled that Stefan would give God his own child.36

The abbot went out to work before anyone else, and he came first to church and stood without leaning on the wall. Late in the evening, especially on the long, dark nights of autumn and winter, he walked past the cells. Where he heard prayer, he thanked God and prayed for the monk inside. Where he heard talk or laughter, he knocked on the door or the window and walked on. In the morning he called the monk to him. He did not scold him in anger. He spoke “indirectly, quietly and gently, as if telling parables,” until the man understood.37

In those first years the monastery often lacked the things it needed most. Once the bread ran out, and the salt with it. Saint Sergius forbade the brothers to go out and beg from lay people in the villages. They were to ask God and wait, and he kept the same rule himself. He waited three days.38

At dawn on the fourth day he took an axe and went to an old monk named Daniil. “Old man, I hear you want to add a porch to your cell,” he said. “I do not want my hands to sit idle, so I have come to you. Let me build the porch.” Daniil agreed, but he feared the price. “I only wait for a carpenter from the village. I do not dare hire you, because you will charge me a lot.”39

Saint Sergius asked only for old, rotten bread. “I take no pay before I have done the work,” he said. He told Daniil to keep the bread until the ninth hour, the time of the Church’s late-day prayers. He worked all day. In the evening Daniil brought out a sieve of old moldy bread and some dry cakes. Saint Sergius set it before himself, prayed, and blessed it. He ate it with water, with no soup, no salt, and nothing else. Some of the brothers watched and saw dust come from his mouth as he ate the spoiled bread.40

The brothers had eaten nothing for two days, and one of them spoke for the rest. “How long will you forbid us to leave and ask lay people for bread? We will bear one more night. In the morning we will leave and not come back, so that we do not die of hunger.” The others came to the abbot with him. “Our bread has gone moldy!” they cried. They had obeyed him, and now they were starving. Saint Sergius reminded them how Christ spoke of the birds, which do not sow or reap and which the heavenly Father feeds.41

“If He feeds the birds, can He not give food to us? Now is the time for patience, and we complain. If we bear this short trial with thanks, the trial itself will do us great good. Even gold is not made pure without fire.”

— Saint Sergius to his monks, in the Life of Sergius by Saint Dimitry of Rostov

He was still speaking when someone knocked at the gate. The gatekeeper looked through the little window and saw a cart full of bread. He was very hungry himself, but in his joy he did not stop to open the gate. He ran to the abbot instead. “Father, bless the men who brought the loaves! Through your prayers they have brought us much food, and it is at the gate.” The brothers opened the gate, saw the cart and the baskets, and praised God. The men who had brought it said only that “a rich man who loved Christ” had sent it to Saint Sergius and the brothers who lived with him. Saint Sergius told the brothers to invite the carriers to the table. But the carriers would not stay, and they hurried away.42

Saint Sergius was as hungry as anyone, and still he did not touch the bread. He had the wooden board struck to call the monks to church, and he led them in to give thanks to God. Only then did he sit down with them. He prayed over the loaves, blessed them, broke them, and shared them out. The bread was still warm and soft.43

A Farmer Mistakes Saint Sergius for a Beggar

Saint Sergius wore clothes of rough, undyed peasant cloth. Once the monastery had a poor piece of cloth, and seven monks in turn refused it. Saint Sergius took it and made himself a robe, and he wore the robe until it fell apart.44

A farmer came from a distant village to see him, and he asked the brothers where the abbot was. Saint Sergius was digging in the vegetable garden, so they sent the man to the fence. Through a gap he saw an old man in a poor robe, torn and patched, digging the ground. The farmer had hoped to see a prophet in great honor and glory, and he thought the monks were mocking him. “I came to see a prophet,” he said, “and you show me an orphan.” “The old man you saw is our abbot,” the brothers told him. When Saint Sergius came out of the garden, the farmer turned his back on him and laughed.45

The brothers were angry and wanted to throw him out, but Saint Sergius would not allow it. He called the farmer over, bowed to the ground before him, and kissed him. He sat him at his right hand and gave him food. The farmer was still unhappy. “Do not be sad, friend,” Saint Sergius told him. “By God’s mercy, no one leaves here sad, and your wish will be granted.”46

As they talked, word came that a prince had arrived with many servants. Saint Sergius went out to meet him. The prince bowed to the ground from far off and asked for his blessing. Then the prince and the old man sat side by side and talked, and the servants pushed the farmer far back. The farmer asked a man nearby who the old man was. “Are you a newcomer here, that you do not know this old man? This is the venerable Sergius.” The farmer began to tremble and blamed himself for his lack of faith. When the prince had gone, he fell at the abbot’s feet and asked forgiveness. Years later he came back and became a monk himself.47

The brothers had their own complaints. As their number grew, water ran short, and they had to carry it from far away. Some of them grumbled at Saint Sergius, not once but many times. “Why did you settle here without thinking, and build a monastery in a place where there is no water?” they asked. When the first monks came years before, he had said that he would accept a monastery “if God has willed it.” Now he spoke as a man who knew.48

“I wanted to live here in silence, alone. But it pleased God to raise up such a monastery in this place, to the glory of His most holy name. Be bold in prayer, and do not lose heart.”

— Saint Sergius to his monks, in the Life of Sergius

God had once brought water out of a rock for His people in the desert, he reminded them. Would He leave them, who worked for Him day and night? Then he took one monk with him and went down into a wooded ravine below the monastery. The old people said no spring had ever run there. He found a little rainwater standing in a ditch, knelt beside it, and prayed. He asked God to show His power here, as He had through Moses in the desert, and to give them water. Then he made the sign of the Cross over the rainwater, and a full spring burst up out of the ground.49

The spring kept running, and the monastery drew its water from it. Sick people who came to it with faith were healed, and some carried its water home to the sick. For ten or fifteen years people called it “Sergius’s spring”, and the name made him angry. “Let me never hear you call this spring by my name,” he said. “I did not give you the water. The Lord gave it to us, unworthy as we are.”50

Far away in Constantinople, the Patriarch had heard of him too.

A Letter From Constantinople Changes the Monastery

One day Greek envoys came to the monastery from Patriarch Saint Philotheus of Constantinople. They brought his blessing and his gifts: a cross, a robe, and a small cloth. The robe was a schema, worn by the strictest rank of monks. The cloth was a paraman, which has a cross on it and is worn on a monk’s back. In those days the monastery itself had no gold or silver, and it lacked even the things it needed. The envoys also brought a letter.51

“By God’s mercy, the Archbishop of Constantinople and Universal Patriarch, lord Philotheus, to Sergius, son and fellow servant of our humility in the Holy Spirit: grace, peace, and our blessing. We heard of your virtuous life by God’s commandments, and we praised God and glorified His name. But one thing, and the most important, is still missing for you: you have no common life.”

— Patriarch Saint Philotheus to Saint Sergius, in the Life of Sergius by Saint Dimitry of Rostov

Until then each monk had kept his own cell and his own things. Saint Sergius did not decide alone. He took the letter to Metropolitan Saint Alexis in Moscow. This was the monk who had once sung in the choir beside Stefan. “Holy master, what do you command?” Saint Sergius asked him. Saint Alexis agreed with the Patriarch and advised a strict common life.52

So Saint Sergius set up the common life. No monk could own anything or call anything his own, and food, clothing, and housing were shared by all. He named brothers to care for the table, the household, the treasury, the sick, and the church. What was left over went to the poor, to guests, and to the sick. He promised that the monastery would stand as long as the brothers kept the works of mercy. The poverty he had chosen for himself in the forest was now the rule of the whole house.53

While Saint Theodore still lived at the Trinity, Saint Sergius once served the Liturgy with him and with Stefan. Prince Vladimir of Serpukhov was staying at the monastery then. In the church was Saint Isaac the Silent, a monk who loved stillness. During the service he saw a fourth priest at the altar, shining so brightly that he could not look at the priest’s face. A second monk named Makarii saw him too. The prince’s people had brought no priest with them. Afterward the two monks pressed their abbot until he told them the truth. It was an angel of the Lord, he said, and an angel served with him whenever he served the Liturgy. He asked them to tell no one while he lived.54

Saint Theodore grew up in his uncle’s monastery and became a priest. In time he asked to found a monastery of his own, and after a long while Saint Sergius blessed him. With that blessing, Saint Theodore built the Simonov monastery by the Moscow River and gave it the common life. As his fame grew, it sometimes troubled his uncle, who prayed without ceasing that his nephew would finish his road without stumbling. Saint Theodore later became Archbishop of Rostov.55

Some time later, trouble came again. The devil put a thought into the minds of some brothers: to reject Saint Sergius as their abbot. One Saturday the evening service was being sung, and Saint Sergius stood at the altar in his priest’s robes. Stefan stood in the choir on the left. Suddenly he asked the monk who led the singing, “Who gave you this book?” “The abbot gave it to me,” the monk said. Stefan cried out in anger. “Who is abbot here? Was it not I who first founded this monastery?” Other unfitting words were spoken too.56

Saint Sergius heard it all at the altar, and he said nothing. When the service ended, he came out of the church and did not go to his cell. No one saw him go. He left the monastery alone and took the road toward Kinela, and night fell while he was still walking. He slept in the wilderness, alone again, as he had once asked God to let him live. In the morning he went on to the monastery at Makhrishche and asked its abbot for a monk to show him the lonely places. The two of them walked through many wild thickets. At last they came to a beautiful place by the river Kirzhach.57

Back at the Trinity, the brothers could not find him anywhere. They were frightened, and they searched the lonely places and the towns. At last one of them learned at Makhrishche where he had gone. They began to come to him at Kirzhach by twos and threes, and sometimes in large groups. He built a cell, and with the blessing of Saint Alexis he built a church. Princes and boyars came and gave silver for the building, and soon many brothers lived there.58

The monks who had stayed at the Trinity went to the Metropolitan. “We live like sheep without a shepherd,” they told him, and they begged him to send their abbot home. Saint Alexis sent two senior abbots to him with a letter. It was enough, he wrote, that Saint Sergius had built a church at Kirzhach and gathered brothers there. Let him put a disciple in his place and return to the monastery of the Holy Trinity. “Those who oppose you I will drive out of the monastery, so that not one who wishes you ill is left there,” the Metropolitan promised. “Only do not disobey us.”59

Saint Sergius gave the envoys his answer. “Tell my lord the Metropolitan: everything that comes from your mouth I will receive with joy, as if it came from the mouth of Christ. I will not disobey you in anything.”60

He chose his disciple Saint Roman to lead the new house, sent him to the Metropolitan to be made a priest, and went home. The whole brotherhood came out to meet him. When they saw him, it seemed to them that a second sun had risen. Some kissed his hands, some his feet, and some the hem of his robe, and some ran ahead to look at him. “Glory to you, O God, who cares for all!” they cried. And he rejoiced in spirit too, seeing his children together again.61

Then Saint Alexis sent for him once more.

Saint Sergius Refuses to Lead the Russian Church

Saint Alexis felt his strength failing and knew his end was near. He wanted Saint Sergius to follow him as Metropolitan. When Saint Sergius came, the Metropolitan held out his own paraman with a gold cross set with precious stones. Saint Sergius bowed and would not take it.62

“Forgive me, holy master. From my youth I have not worn gold, and in old age I want even more to stay in poverty.”

— Saint Sergius to Metropolitan Saint Alexis, in the Life of Sergius by Saint Dimitry of Rostov

“Beloved, I know you have always lived so,” Saint Alexis answered. “Now show obedience and accept the blessing we give you.” With his own hands he put the paraman on Saint Sergius. Then he told him why he had called him. He had led the Russian Church as long as God willed, he said, and now he wanted to find a man who could shepherd it after him. He found no one but Saint Sergius. “I know well that everyone wants you, from the prince to the last man. So accept the rank of bishop now, and after my death you will take my seat.”63

Saint Sergius was greatly troubled. To him the rank of bishop would be a great misfortune. “Forgive me, master. This is beyond my strength. You will never find in me what you seek. I am a sinner and the last of all people.” Saint Alexis pressed him for a long time and quoted Scripture to him. Saint Sergius would not bend. “Holy master, if you do not want to drive me out of this land, so that you hear nothing more of me, do not speak of this again. Let no one else speak to me so. No one will find me willing.”64

Saint Alexis said no more. He was afraid that Saint Sergius would flee to some far wilderness, and that Moscow would lose such a light. He comforted him with words of the spirit and sent him back to his monastery in peace.65

Saint Alexis reposed on 12 February 1378. He had sung beside Stefan in the choir. He had advised Saint Sergius about the common life, and he had called him home from Kirzhach as a father calls a son. Now the grand princes begged Saint Sergius again to become Metropolitan. He stood “firm as a diamond.”66

Soon a greater fear came over the whole Russian land.

Saint Sergius Blesses the Prince Before Battle

Word came that a prince of the Horde named Mamai had gathered all the Tatar armies and was marching on Russia. The people were seized with fear. Grand Prince Saint Dmitri Ivanovich of Moscow had great faith in Saint Sergius and believed he had the gift of seeing what was to come. He rode to the monastery and asked him one question: did Saint Sergius tell him to go out against the godless? Saint Sergius blessed him, armed him with prayer, and answered.67

“It is right, my lord, that you care for the Christian flock God has given you. Go against the godless. With God helping you, you will win, and you will come back to your own land safe, with great honor.”

— Saint Sergius to Grand Prince Saint Dmitri, in the Life of Sergius

“If God helps me, Father, I will build a monastery in the name of the Most Pure Mother of God,” the prince vowed. He took the blessing and left in haste.68

Saint Dmitri gathered all his men and marched. In September 1380 the Russians reached the Kulikovo field by the river Don. There they saw the Tatar host and how great it was, and they stopped in doubt. Many were afraid. At that very hour a runner arrived with a letter from Saint Sergius. “Without any doubt, my lord, go boldly against their fierceness. Do not be afraid at all. God will surely help you.”69

The prince and his whole army took heart. Saint Dmitri prayed to the great God, who made heaven and earth, to help him against the enemies of His holy name. Then the battle began, and many men fell. The Tatars were beaten and fled.70

Many days’ walk away, Saint Sergius stood in prayer with his brothers, and he saw the battle as if it were near. A little later he told them of the victory. Then he named the fallen Russian men one by one and prayed for the repose of their souls.71

Saint Dmitri came back to the monastery to thank him and gave it a rich gift. Then he reminded the abbot of his vow to build a monastery for the Most Pure Mother of God, and said he wanted to begin at once. Saint Sergius went out to find a place, and on the river Dubenka he built a church of the Dormition of the Mother of God, named for her falling asleep. He made his disciple Saint Savva its abbot. Another time the prince asked him to bless a place for a monastery at Golutvin, near Kolomna. Saint Sergius went there on foot, as he always traveled, and built the church. When Prince Vladimir of Serpukhov asked for a monastery too, Saint Sergius gave him his disciple Saint Athanasius to lead it, though he loved Saint Athanasius very much.72

Saint Dmitri often came to Saint Sergius for counsel and for blessing, and he asked him to stand as godfather to his children. The prince of Ryazan would make no peace with Moscow. In 1385 Saint Sergius went to Ryazan as Saint Dmitri’s envoy. He talked with the angry prince for a long time about the soul, about peace, and about love. His quiet and gentle words moved the prince, who agreed to a lasting peace. Saint Dmitri reposed in 1389.73

Through all these years, one prayer stayed with Saint Sergius. He prayed for his monastery and for the men in it.

The Mother of God Visits Saint Sergius

Once Saint Sergius stood before an icon of the Mother of God in his cell, saying his usual prayers. He looked at the icon again and again as he prayed. He sang the akathist, the long hymn of praise to her. Then he prayed in his own words.74

“Most Pure Mother of my Christ, mediator and defender, strong helper of the human race!” He asked her to protect him and his brothers, unworthy as they were, and to pray to her Son for that holy place. The man who had once asked God to let him live without a single person near him now prayed for his disciples.75

When he had finished, he sat down to rest a little. His disciple Saint Micah was with him. “Child, be sober and keep watch,” Saint Sergius said, “for a wondrous and fearful visit is about to come to us in this hour.”76

He had hardly spoken when a voice was heard: “Look, the Most Pure One is coming!” Saint Sergius rose and went quickly out of his cell into the porch. A great light fell on him, brighter than the sun. In that light he saw the Mother of God with the apostles Saint Peter and Saint John. They shone in a light that no words can tell. He fell on his face. He could not bear that brightness.77

She touched him with her hands and spoke.

“Do not be afraid, my chosen one. I have come to visit you. Your prayer for your disciples and for your monastery has been heard. Do not grieve any more, because from now on it will have plenty of everything. Not only in your life, but after you go to the Lord, I will not leave your monastery. I will give what it needs without lack, and I will keep it and cover it.”

— The Mother of God to Saint Sergius, in the Life of Sergius

Then she was gone. Saint Sergius was seized with fear and trembling, and for a while he was beside himself. When he came to himself he found Saint Micah lying on the floor as if dead from fear. He lifted him up. Saint Micah threw himself at the abbot’s feet and asked what the vision had been. His spirit had nearly left his body, he said. Saint Sergius’s face glowed with joy, but he could not answer yet. “Wait, child, for my spirit also trembles at the wondrous vision.”78

After a while he sent Saint Micah for two more disciples, Isaac and Simon. When they came, he told them everything in order. Together they sang a service of prayer to the Mother of God and gave glory to God. Saint Sergius did not sleep for the rest of that night.79

The Repose of Saint Sergius

Six months before his death, Saint Sergius knew that his departure was near. He called the brothers and gave the care of the monastery to his beloved disciple Saint Nikon, “young in body but gray-haired in mind.” He told Saint Nikon to feed the flock with care, because he would answer for many souls. From then on Saint Sergius kept silence.80

In September he fell ill. He called his brothers once more and taught them for the last time. He told them to hold to the Orthodox faith and to be of one mind. He told them to keep their souls and bodies pure, to love without pretending, and above all to clothe themselves in humility. They were not to forget hospitality, and they were to count the honor and glory of this life as nothing. Then he spoke his last words to them.81

“God is calling me, and I am going away from you. I give you to the Almighty Lord and to his Most Pure Mother. Let her be your refuge and a wall against the snares of the enemy and his barking.”

— Saint Sergius’s last words to his monks, in the Life of Sergius

At the very end he received the Body and Blood of the Lord, while his disciples held up his weak limbs with their hands. Then he raised his hands to heaven and prayed. With that prayer he gave his soul to the Lord and went to “the desired Jesus.” Saint Sergius reposed on 25 September 1392.82

A great fragrance poured from his body, and the brothers wept. They laid him on a bier and carried him out with psalms and funeral prayers, and they buried him in the monastery he had founded. His face shone like snow. It looked like the face of a living man or of an angel of God, and nothing like the face of the dead.83

Monks Find Saint Sergius’s Body Whole

Thirty years later, God chose to glorify His servant. A man who lived near the monastery often prayed at Saint Sergius’s grave. One night he fell into a light sleep as he prayed there, and Saint Sergius appeared to him. “Why do you leave me so long in the grave, covered with earth? The water presses on my body!” He told the man to tell the abbot. The man woke afraid and glad at once and went straight to Saint Nikon, and Saint Nikon told the brothers.84

Princes gathered, and a council of clergy with them. Among them was Saint Dmitri’s son Prince Yury, whom Saint Sergius himself had baptized. They opened the grave, and the place filled with fragrance. The body was whole and bright, and the robe was whole too. Water stood on both sides of the grave, but it had not touched the body or the robe. They gave glory to God. On 5 July 1422, with psalms and singing, they laid his holy relics in a shrine, where the sick who came with faith received healing.85

Over the grave Saint Nikon built a church of stone, dedicated to the Holy Trinity, and he had it painted by two old masters, Daniil and Andrei. The Church remembers this Andrei as Saint Andrei Rublev. Between 1425 and 1427 a workshop of masters under Saint Andrei Rublev and Daniil painted the church’s icons and frescoes. Its chief icon was the Holy Trinity, which Saint Andrei Rublev painted “in praise of Saint Sergius.”86

By then his Life had been written. Saint Epiphanius the Wise was a monk of the monastery, and he had gathered stories for many years. Some came from Saint Sergius himself. Others came from Stefan, the brother who had helped him carry the first logs. Saint Epiphanius wrote the Life in 1417 and 1418. In 1449 or 1450 Metropolitan Saint Jona of Moscow named Saint Sergius among the wonderworkers in a letter, and the Russian Church glorified him as a saint around that time. His people had honored him long before.87

The Monastery Saint Sergius Left Behind

Saint Sergius wrote no books. He left the Church a way of life: the common life, in which no monk owns anything. He also left men who carried it into new monasteries, and their disciples carried it farther still. Russians pray to him as the patron of their land. Students and teachers pray to him too, because of the boy who could not learn his letters until he met the stranger under the oak.88

The Mother of God had promised not to leave his monastery after he was gone. Two hundred years later an army laid siege to it, from 1608 to 1610. A chief of the enemy soldiers named Andrei and the men under him wished to repent, and they fled from the enemy camp. They swore an oath by God’s name and told what they had seen before one attack. A fast river had flowed between them and the walls, where no river runs. Two gray-haired old men had stood on the walls and shouted at them. The defenders inside knew nothing of this, but the attack failed. Saint Sergius had appeared to them, and by his prayers God gave the monastery victory over its enemies.89

In April 1919 the Soviet government opened his shrine, and the shrine was given to a museum set up in the closed monastery. In 1941 it was sent far away to Solikamsk, and it came back in 1944.90

On 20 April 1946 the state gave his holy relics back to the Church. That day was Holy Saturday, the eve of Easter. Today they rest again in the Trinity church that Saint Nikon built over his grave. It stands in the monastery that grew where Saint Sergius once lived alone, without a single person near him.91

A Note on the Sources

Saint Epiphanius the Wise wrote the Life of Saint Sergius in 1417 and 1418, and Pachomius the Serb reworked it between 1440 and 1459. Saint Epiphanius’s own text does not survive on its own. The story here follows the old Life in two forms: a modern Russian translation and an Old Russian compilation of the sixteenth century. It also follows Saint Dimitry of Rostov’s retelling of the 1690s. The chapter on the finding of the relics is credited in the edition used here to Simon Azarin in 1646, although its introduction says Pachomius first told that story. The edition’s editors date the finding to 1423; most accounts give 1422. In the Life, only his death has a year; his birth has none. Scholars place the birth in 1314 or in 1322, and the editors doubt the Life’s age of seventy-eight.

The Life names no battle in the war with Mamai and gives no year. Later works link the blessing to the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380. One is the Tale of the Rout of Mamai, which the editors date most likely to the first quarter of the fifteenth century. Another is Saint Dimitry of Rostov’s Life. Both have the holy water and the two warrior monks, Saint Peresvet and Saint Oslyabya, whom the old Life does not mention. The historian V. A. Kuchkin has argued that the blessing belongs before the battle on the Vozha River in 1378, and the writer Dmitry Volodikhin defends the traditional view. In the oldest text the blessing says “God helping you”; later texts turn it into a firm promise.

Saint Dimitry of Rostov places Stefan’s outburst after the common life began. He suggests that the brothers resented its strictness and that Stefan wanted power. Those guesses are left out here. The Life does not say how Stefan’s life ended. Saint Dmitri’s death year comes from the editors’ notes, and the peace mission to Ryazan in 1385 from Saint Dimitry of Rostov. The editors’ note counts Saint Isaac the Silent as a saint; the Isaac who heard of the Mother of God’s visit may be another monk. The Orthodox Encyclopedia identifies the painter Andrei as Saint Andrei Rublev, on the basis of Pachomius’s Life of Saint Nikon. Church tradition holds that the saint’s head was hidden before the 1919 opening and returned in 1946. The Soviet record of that day describes bones and a skull. In the sixteenth century Saint Maxim the Greek questioned whether Saint Sergius was a saint. His reason was that Saint Sergius and the hierarchs of Moscow held towns, villages, and wealth.

How This Life Was Researched

This Life rests on eleven sources: two in Old Russian, eight in modern Russian, and one in English. The oldest is the Life by Saint Epiphanius the Wise. It was read in a sixteenth-century Old Russian compilation and in a modern Russian translation of the eighty-eight-chapter version, and about twenty-five of its chapters were read closely. Beside it stand Saint Dimitry of Rostov’s Life of the 1690s and the Tale of the Rout of Mamai. A study printed in 1922, an encyclopedia, the Lavra’s own pages, and two church magazine articles fill in the rest. The research notes mark nine facts as likely missing from popular English pages, among them the violence at Rostov, the night rounds, the hunger, and the farmer at the fence.

saint.relic_description: Sergius died on 25 September 1392 and was buried at his Trinity monastery. Hegumen Nikon opened the grave before princes and a council; the body and robe were reported whole, and the relics were placed in a shrine on 5 July, in the year 1422 according to modern scholarship. Nikon then built a stone Trinity church. On 11 April 1919, under a Soviet decree of 1 February 1919, a commission opened the shrine and recorded bones, fragments of a rotted robe (the foot bones had crumbled away), and a lock of fair-reddish hair wrapped in recent waxed paper in the skull; the protocol was signed by those present, including Archimandrite Kronid, and Lev Kuleshov filmed the opening. Church tradition holds that Pavel Florensky and Count Yury Olsufiev had secretly removed the head beforehand and replaced it with the skull of a Prince Trubetskoy, and that the head was hidden at Vinogradovo and rejoined the relics in 1946; The shrine became a museum exhibit, was evacuated to Solikamsk from 25 July 1941 to 19 November 1944, and on Holy Saturday, 20 April 1946, the relics were returned to the Church and moved to the Dormition cathedral. They now rest in the Trinity cathedral of the Lavra.

miracles.miracles:
The Church remembers Saint Sergius of Radonezh as a man through whom God worked many wonders, in his life and at his tomb. This list gathers those wonders as the Life of Saint Sergius tells them. Each account names who told it and when.

Most come from the Life of Saint Sergius, which his disciple Saint Epiphanius the Wise wrote in 1417 and 1418. That Life has come down to us in the form that the monk Pachomius the Serb gave it between 1440 and 1459. He added the finding of the relics and the first miracles at the tomb. In 1646 Simon Azarin added the miracles of later years. Each status line says which of these writers tells the account.

The Russian Church glorified Saint Sergius as a saint in the fifteenth century. To glorify a saint is the Orthodox Church’s act of naming a person a saint before the whole Church. The people honored him before the Church had written rules for this, so no single document gives the date. Saint Sergius himself asked the witnesses of several of these wonders to keep silent while he lived.

During Saint Sergius’s Life

Saint Sergius cries out three times before birth

Saint Sergius’s mother Saint Maria stood in church at the Sunday Liturgy, the Church’s main service. The child in her womb cried out at the Gospel reading and again at the start of the hymn that goes with the bringing of the bread and wine. He cried a third time at the priest’s call before Holy Communion, “Holy Things for the Holy.” The women nearby asked what this child would be. Years later his brother Stefan told Saint Sergius to name the forest church for the Holy Trinity because of the three cries.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, chs. 2 and 5, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

A baby who refuses milk on fast days

Saint Sergius was given the name Bartholomew at his baptism. As a baby he would not take his mother’s milk on Wednesdays and Fridays, which are the Church’s fast days. He also refused milk on days when his mother had eaten meat. He would not take milk from any other nurse.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 2, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

God gives Saint Sergius the gift of reading

Saint Sergius was sent to school at seven and struggled to learn his letters. He prayed to God in tears for help. One day his father sent him to look for some foals, and the boy found an old man in a black robe praying under an oak. The boy asked for his prayers, and the old man gave him a piece of holy bread that tasted sweet as honey. He told the boy that from that day the Lord would give him the knowledge of letters. At home the boy read the Psalms clearly and well, and his parents and brothers praised God. The old man said that the boy would be “a dwelling of the Holy Trinity” and then vanished at the gate. The parents believed that the old man was an angel, sent to give the boy the knowledge of letters.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, chs. 2–3, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

Fragrance fills the church at Saint Sergius’s vows

The abbot Mitrofan made Saint Sergius a monk on 7 October. The Church keeps that day for Saints Sergius and Bacchus, so the new monk was given the name Sergius. After he received Holy Communion, the church filled with fragrance. The Life says he was twenty-three.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 6, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

Demons break into the forest church

Saint Sergius went into his forest church at night to sing Matins, the early morning service. The wall opened, and demons in Lithuanian clothes and tall pointed caps rushed in and threatened to kill him if he did not leave. Saint Sergius used prayer, the Psalms, and the precious Cross as his weapons, and the demons vanished at once. He thanked God. A few days later many demons shouted at him during all-night prayer in his hut. God’s power scattered them. Saint Epiphanius thought that it took less than an hour.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 7, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

Wolves and bears leave him unharmed

Wild animals often came to Saint Sergius in the forest, by night and by day. Wolves came in packs, howling and roaring, and sometimes bears came. Saint Sergius feared them a little, like any person. He prayed to God with all his heart, and the animals did him no harm.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 6, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

A bear waits for bread at a stump

A bear came to Saint Sergius to find food, not to harm him. Saint Sergius laid a small piece of bread on a stump or log, and the bear took it and went away. When there was no bread, the bear stood and looked around for a long time, like a hard lender who wants his debt paid. When Saint Sergius had only one piece, he broke it in two. Sometimes he gave the bear all of it and went hungry. This went on for more than a year.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 7, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

Fresh bread arrives at the gate after hunger

The monastery ran out of bread and salt, and Saint Sergius told the brothers not to beg but to ask God and wait. He waited three days, and on the fourth morning he took an axe and built a porch for an old monk named Daniil. Daniil paid him with a sieve of old, spoiled bread, and Saint Sergius blessed it and ate it with water. The hungry brothers threatened to leave. While Saint Sergius was still speaking to them, a cart of fresh warm loaves arrived at the gate. The gatekeeper ran to him: “Father, bless the men who brought the loaves! Through your prayers they have brought us much food.” The men said that a rich man who loved Christ had sent it from far away, and then they left. Before anyone ate, Saint Sergius led the brothers into church to sing a service of thanks to God. Then he blessed the loaves and shared them out, and the brothers praised God, who had fed them.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18). The Life tells it as God’s care for His servants, and it does not name the giver.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 10, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

A spring rises at Saint Sergius’s prayer

The community grew and had no water nearby, and the brothers asked Saint Sergius why he had settled there. He told them to pray and not lose heart, because God had once brought water from a rock for Israel in the desert. Then he went down to a ravine with one monk and knelt beside a ditch that held a little rainwater. He prayed to God to show His glory and give them water in that place. He made the sign of the Cross over the water, and a full spring broke out of the ground. It was still in use when the Life was written, and the monks drew from it with thanks to God. Many sick people were healed by its water when they came to it with faith, and the Life says this went on in its own day. For ten or fifteen years people called it Saint Sergius’s spring. He was angry and told them that the Lord had given the water, not he.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 12, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

A dead child lives again at the monastery

A man who lived near the monastery carried his sick baby son to Saint Sergius, and the child died while the father was asking for prayer. The father went out to get a coffin. Saint Sergius had pity on him. He knelt and prayed for the dead child, and the child came back to life. When the father returned, he found his son alive and fell at the saint’s feet to thank him. Saint Sergius told him that the boy had only been cold and had warmed up in the cell. He said that no one can rise before the resurrection of all the dead, and he told the father to tell no one. The father did not dare to spread the story, but he could not stay silent about it either. In his heart he praised God. The story became known through one of Saint Sergius’s disciples.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18). The Life’s chapter title calls it a raising from the dead, and Saint Sergius himself said that the boy was only cold.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 13, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

A nobleman tormented by a demon is healed

A nobleman from far away on the Volga River was tormented day and night by a demon. He broke iron chains, and ten strong men could not hold him. His family heard what God was doing through Saint Sergius, and they took him to the monastery. On the way he screamed that he did not want to see the saint. When Saint Sergius heard that the man was near, he gathered the brothers in church and sang a service of prayer for him. Then he came out of the church with a cross in his hand, and the man cried out and threw himself into a pool of rainwater. He said later that he had seen great flames come from the cross. From that moment his mind was clear, by the grace of Christ and the prayers of the saint. He stayed a few days at the monastery and went home well, praising God, who had healed him.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Pachomius the Serb revised (1440–59).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 14, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

An angel serves with Saint Sergius at Liturgy

Saint Sergius served the Liturgy with his brother and his nephew while Prince Vladimir was a guest at the monastery. A monk named Isaac the Silent saw a fourth priest at the altar, shining brighter than the sun and following behind Saint Sergius. A monk named Makarii also saw him, and the monks learned that the prince’s party had brought no priest. Saint Sergius first said that only three priests had served. Then he told them that an angel of the Lord served with him whenever he served, and that they must tell no one while he lived.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 21, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

Saint Sergius foretells Michael’s death at sea

Metropolitan Saint Alexis died in 1378, and the princes asked Saint Sergius to take his place as head of the Russian Church. Saint Sergius refused. A senior abbot named Michael took the seat instead and turned against him. Saint Sergius told his disciples that Michael would not get what he wanted and would not even see Constantinople, because pride had overcome him. Michael fell ill and died on the sea voyage to Constantinople. The Life says that after this everyone counted Saint Sergius among the prophets.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18). The edition’s note dates Michael’s death to 1379.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 25 and note 87, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

Saint Sergius sees a battle from far away

Saint Sergius was praying with his brothers at the hour of Grand Prince Saint Dmitri’s battle with Mamai, the Tatar leader. From a place many days’ walk away he saw the fight. A little later he told the brothers of Saint Dmitri’s courage and said that the Russians had won. He named the men who had fallen and prayed for them. The Life does not name the battle, and later writers place it at Kulikovo in 1380.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Pachomius the Serb revised (1440–59). See the note at the end.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 22, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com; “Sergii Radonezhsky,” Russian Wikipedia.

The Mother of God appears to Saint Sergius

Saint Sergius stood before an icon of the Most Holy Mother of God and prayed for his monastery. He sang the akathist, a hymn of praise to her. Then he told his disciple Saint Micah to stay alert. A voice said, “Look, the Most Pure One is coming!” Saint Sergius went out to the porch and saw her in a light brighter than the sun, with the apostles Saint Peter and Saint John. She touched him and said, “Do not be afraid, my chosen one. I have come to visit you. Do not grieve, for your prayer for your disciples and your monastery has been heard. … In your life and after you go to God, I will not leave this place.” Saint Micah lay on the floor as if dead from fear. Saint Sergius later told the whole story to two other disciples, Isaac and Simon. Together they sang a service of prayer to the Mother of God and gave glory to God.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18). The Lavra keeps 24 August (6 September on the modern calendar) in memory of the appearance.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 26, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com; “Sergii Radonezhsky,” Russian Wikipedia.

Fire enters the chalice at the Liturgy

Simon was the disciple who had heard of the Mother of God’s visit, and he was in charge of the church. During the Liturgy that Saint Sergius served, Simon saw fire move around the altar. The fire folded like a veil and entered the chalice, and Saint Sergius received Holy Communion from it. Saint Sergius called Simon over and asked why he was afraid, and Simon told him what he had seen. Saint Sergius told him to tell no one until after his own death.

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 31, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

A flock of birds promises many disciples

Saint Sergius was praying for his brothers late one evening when a voice called his name. A light brighter than day filled the night, and he saw a great flock of beautiful birds around the monastery. The voice said that the Lord had received his prayer for his spiritual children. His disciples would be as many as the birds, and they would not dwindle after him if they followed in his footsteps. Saint Sergius called his disciple Simon, who saw only a gleam of the light. Saint Sergius then told him all that he had seen and heard, and they rejoiced together.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Pachomius the Serb revised (1440–59).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 14, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

A bright face and fragrance at Saint Sergius’s death

Saint Sergius reposed in the Lord on 25 September 1392, which is 8 October on today’s civil calendar. He had received Holy Communion, and his disciples held him up while he raised his hands and prayed. A great fragrance came from his body. The Life says his face was bright, “not like a dead man’s.”

Status: told by Saint Epiphanius the Wise in his Life of Saint Sergius (1417–18).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise and Pachomius Logothetes, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 32, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

After Saint Sergius’s Death

Saint Sergius’s body is found whole after thirty years

The Life says that thirty years after Saint Sergius’s death, God chose to glorify His servant still more. A man who lived near the monastery often prayed at Saint Sergius’s grave. Saint Sergius appeared to him in a dream and asked, “Why do you leave me so long in the grave, covered with earth? The water presses on my body!” The man told the abbot Saint Nikon. Princes and a council of clergy gathered, and the council opened the grave. The place filled with fragrance. The body and the robe were whole. Water stood on both sides of the grave, but it had not touched them. Everyone gave glory to God. On 5 July they placed his holy relics in a shrine with psalms and singing. Relics are the saint’s body, which the Church keeps with honor. The Life says that the relics rest in the shrine to this day and give healing to the sick who come to them with faith.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapter on the finding of the relics. Pachomius the Serb first told the story, and Simon Azarin wrote the chapter in its present form in 1646. The Church keeps 5 July (18 July on the modern calendar) as the feast of the finding of the relics, in 1422. See the note at the end.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise, Pachomius Logothetes, and Simon Azarin, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 33 and notes 92–95, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also “Sergii Radonezhsky,” Russian Wikipedia.

Saint Sergius guides two travelers through a fortress

A priest named Symeon suffered in chains for opposing Metropolitan Isidore at a Church council in the West. Symeon and an envoy from Tver ran away toward Russia and lay down to rest on a mountain road near a fortress of robbers. In a dream an old man told Symeon that he would stay with them and lead them through the fortress without harm, and he said that he was Saint Sergius. At the fortress the travelers prayed, “Holy Sergius, cover us and help us!” Someone opened the iron gates for them and said nothing, and the gates closed again behind them. They reached Russia, and Symeon told the monastery’s brothers the whole story with tears. All of them glorified God and His saint.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Pachomius the Serb revised (1440–59). Saint Dimitry of Rostov gave a shorter version of it, without the fortress.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise, Pachomius Logothetes, and Simon Azarin, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 47, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

A mute young man speaks at the tomb

A young man from Yaroslavl came to Saint Sergius’s holy relics unable to speak. He kissed the relics and at once spoke clearly. Then he told how two years earlier he had woken blind on Great Friday. A year later his sight had returned, but his speech had gone. Then he heard of the miracles of Saint Sergius, and he came with faith.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Pachomius the Serb revised (1440–59).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise, Pachomius Logothetes, and Simon Azarin, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 51, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

A tormented boy is healed at the tomb

A boy from a noble family of Ryazan was tormented by an unclean spirit. He cut his clothes to pieces, and no one could calm him. At the tomb of Saint Sergius he was healed. He did not go home but became a monk at the monastery and helped the brothers with their work until he died.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Pachomius the Serb revised (1440–59).

Source: Epiphanius the Wise, Pachomius Logothetes, and Simon Azarin, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 52, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

Attackers see a river and old men, 1608–10

Lithuanian regiments laid siege to the monastery from September 1608 to January 1610. The Life says that God gave the monastery victory through the prayers of Saint Sergius. A chief of soldiers named Andrei ran away from those regiments with his men, and they swore in God’s name before they told what they had seen. Before one assault they saw a fast river between them and the monastery, though no river ran there. Two gray-haired old men on the walls shouted at them. The men inside the monastery did not know about this, and the assault failed with many dead among the attackers. Andrei said that the Lord had spared him and his men so that they would repent.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Simon Azarin added in 1646. The chapter is taken from the story of the siege by Avraamy Palitsyn. He was the monastery’s cellarer, the monk in charge of its stores.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise, Pachomius Logothetes, and Simon Azarin, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 63 and notes 134–138, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

Cossacks see the monastery at sea, 1622

In 1622 a Don Cossack leader named Epifan Radilov came to the Trinity monastery with seventy men to keep a vow. They brought two silver-gilt cups as a gift to the Lord and to the saints. They told the abbot that the Turks had begun to win a sea battle against them. The Cossacks had prayed to the Holy Trinity and the Most Pure Mother of God, and they had called on Saint Sergius and Saint Nikon. They promised to visit the monastery if God gave them victory through the saints’ prayers. The Lord showed them His mercy at once. Many of them saw the monastery appear before them, and they took heart, attacked, and beat the Turks.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Simon Azarin added in 1646.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise, Pachomius Logothetes, and Simon Azarin, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 74, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

A soldier is healed at the tomb, 1632

In 1632 a sick soldier was brought to Saint Sergius’s tomb while painters were decorating the Trinity church. He screamed because his head and hands were cramping. After a service of prayer his health and mind returned, by the grace of Christ and the prayers of the saint. He left praising God and His saint.

Status: told in the Life of Saint Sergius, in the chapters that Simon Azarin added in 1646.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise, Pachomius Logothetes, and Simon Azarin, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, ch. 75, modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru.

Other miracles in the Life, chapters 34–88

The later Life has 55 chapters after the finding of the relics, numbered 34 to 88. Most tell of miracles. Their titles name healings of the blind and the mute, victories in war, and appearances of Saint Sergius in Moscow and Kazan. Two chapters tell of other things: the death of Abbot Saint Nikon and a word of praise to Saint Sergius. Saint Dimitry of Rostov wrote that many healings were given through the holy relics and that healings still flowed from the shrine in his own day.

Status: told in the later chapters of the Life, by Pachomius the Serb and Simon Azarin. See the note at the end.

Source: Epiphanius the Wise, Pachomius Logothetes, and Simon Azarin, Life and Miracles of Sergius of Radonezh, chs. 34–88 (chapter list), modern Russian translation, Azbyka.ru; also Dimitry of Rostov, “Life of Our Venerable Father Sergius of Radonezh,” English translation, johnsanidopoulos.com.

Saint Sergius’s shrine is opened in 1919

On 11 April 1919 a Soviet commission opened the shrine of Saint Sergius at the Trinity monastery, with Church representatives present. Kronid was the monastery’s deputy head, and he signed the record of what they found. The record lists bones and a rotted robe. In the skull lay a lock of fair reddish hair, wrapped in waxed paper of recent make. Church tradition says that Pavel Florensky and Count Yury Olsufiev had secretly taken the saint’s head before the opening and put another skull in its place. The tradition says the head was returned to the holy relics in 1946.

Status: a historical record rather than a miracle. This entry stands here because it tells what was found when the shrine was opened. The commission’s record and the Church’s tradition about the head differ, and both are given here as they are told.

Source: “Sergii Radonezhsky,” Russian Wikipedia, which cites the Soviet journal Revolution and Church (1919).

A Note on the Sources

The Life names no battle in the war with Mamai and gives no year. Two later works place the blessing of Saint Dmitri before the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380: the Tale of the Rout of Mamai and Saint Dimitry of Rostov’s Life. The historian V. A. Kuchkin has argued that it belongs before the battle on the Vozha River in 1378. Most accounts give the year of the finding of the relics as 1422, and the editors of the Russian edition give 1423. Of the chapters after the finding of the relics, only those told above were read in full for this list. The rest are known from their titles.

teachings.teachings:
Sergius left no writings. Only spiritual instructions remembered by his disciples are known, so what follows is the example of his life as his biographer Epiphanius recorded it, arranged by theme. It is the example of a life, not a body of his own doctrine. The translations from Russian are our own.

Poverty Chosen Freely

Sergius chose poverty and kept it all his life. He gave his whole inheritance to his younger brother Petr before he went into the forest. As hegumen he wore sermyaga, the coarse undyed cloth of peasants, and once took a piece of cloth that seven monks had refused and wore it until it fell apart. A visiting plowman took him for an orphan. When Metropolitan Alexis, near death, gave him a jeweled gold cross and offered him the metropolitan see, he refused.

“Forgive me, master: from my youth I have not been a gold-bearer.”

— Sergius to Metropolitan Alexis, Life of Sergius, chapter 25 (our translation)

He added that in old age he wished to stay poor. Alexis died in 1378, and Sergius remained hegumen of his forest monastery.

Work With One’s Own Hands

The hegumen of Trinity worked first and hardest. With his brother Stefan he cut logs and carried them on his shoulders to build the first church. As hegumen he was first at work and first in church, and he stood through the services without leaning on the wall. Visitors found him digging the garden. When the monastery was hungry, he took an axe and built a porch for an old monk in exchange for bread. Newcomers wore a black coat and did every kind of labor for a long time before they received the habit.

A Common Life

At first each monk at Trinity lived in his own cell and kept his own things. Patriarch Philotheus of Constantinople sent Sergius a letter saying that one rule was missing: the monastery had no common life. With the agreement of Metropolitan Alexis, Sergius introduced a common rule, with a cellarer, cooks, bakers, and an infirmarian, and no private property for anyone. His disciples carried this life to other monasteries, among them Kirzhach, Simonov, Dubenka, Golutvin, and Vysoky.

Trust in God in Want

Sergius warned every newcomer that the forest offered hunger, thirst, and poverty, and told them to prepare their hearts for patience and many trials, not for food, drink, or rest. When the bread ran out, he forbade begging and waited. On the fourth day he worked for a sieve of moldy bread, and while the brothers grumbled, fresh loaves arrived at the gate from a benefactor whose name the brothers never learned. He told the hungry monks to feed the men who had carried the bread first. The same trust shows in the letter he sent to Grand Prince Dmitri when the army stopped in doubt before the Tatar host:

“Without any doubt, lord, go boldly against their fierceness.”

— Sergius to Grand Prince Dmitri, from the Life as quoted in A. P. Rogovich, 1922 (our translation)

Hiding God’s Gifts

Sergius did everything he could to keep praise away from himself. When people called the spring in the ravine by his name, he was angry: the Lord had given the water, he said, not he. When a dead child lived again after his prayer, he told the father the boy had only been cold, and forbade him to tell. He asked Isaac and Makarii to keep the angel at the altar secret while he lived, and Simon to say nothing of the fire in the chalice until after his death.

Correction Without Anger

At night Sergius walked past the cells. Where he heard prayer, he blessed it; where he heard talk or laughter, he knocked on the door or window and went on. The next morning he spoke to the brothers concerned quietly and gently, “from afar,” as Epiphanius says, as if telling parables, and never in anger. When the monks grumbled against him over hunger and over water, he answered with patience and with prayer.

His Last Charge

When he fell ill in September 1392, Sergius gathered the brothers and told them to keep the Orthodox faith and unity among themselves, to keep themselves pure, to welcome strangers, to avoid quarrels, and not to seek honors. He entrusted them to the Lord Almighty and to His Most Pure Mother, whom he called their refuge and wall against the snares of the enemy. Six months earlier he had already handed the monastery to his disciple Nikon.

gaps: Birth year is disputed: 1314 (age 78 in the Life; Borisov) or 1322 (earlier line, about 70; Kuchkin, Kloss); Nikon’s 19th-c. Life gives 1319. birth_year is left null under the Directus rule for disputed dates.

Life chapters 34–88 (the posthumous miracles) were known mainly from their chapter titles, with chapters 58 and 74 skimmed; the miracles list summarizes them only briefly. Chapters 2–33 were checked against the Russian text. The founding chapters for Kirzhach, Andronikov, Simonov, Golutvin, and Vysoky are named but not told in full.

The claim that the Roman martyrology added Sergius in 1969 rests only on Russian Wikipedia and is left out; feast_day_catholic is null and venerated_in is orthodox only. A Catholic primary source could change this.
The hill name “Makovets” and the founding date of the Trinity monastery (1337 or 1342) are not in the sources read and are not stated.

The Kulikovo link, the year 1380, and the monks Peresvet and Oslyabya come from the later Tale of the Mamai Rout (and from Rogovich, who repeats them), which was not itself read; the biography attributes them. The earliest wording of the blessing (“if God helps”) is known from Russian Wikipedia’s quotation of Epiphanius, not from a raw text of Epiphanius. Kuchkin’s link to the Vozha (1378) is given as a scholar’s view.
The birds vision is in Life ch. 14 and in Dimitry of Rostov’s Life; the biography tells it from the Life.
Varnitsy as birthplace rests on Russian Wikipedia; the Life says only a village in the Rostov principality.

The head-switch story (Florensky, Olsufiev) is church tradition as reported by Russian Wikipedia; the 1919 protocol was not read directly and is known from Russian Wikipedia’s description (bones, robe fragments, a skull with a lock of hair). Both accounts are given.

Only 4 block quotes in the biography (aim 6–12): the Life is available only in a modern translation marked facts-only, which allows at most two short block quotes, and the only public-domain wording in the notes is Rogovich 1922.
Only 3 quote records (aim 10–30): the notes hold few exact words of Sergius himself; most of his recorded sayings are marked as paraphrases and cannot be quoted.
Biography is about 5,500 words, near the floor of tier B; the notes do not support more without padding.

Unopened Sanidopoulos pages (relics uncovering 1422; miracles of Sergius and Nikon; resource page), pravenc.ru, drevo-info, and the Great Menaion Reader text could add posthumous miracles and quotations.
Disciples named as saints (Nikon, Savva, Andronikus, Micah, Athanasius of Serpukhov) rest on Russian Wikipedia’s captions and saints template, not on a Church calendar read directly.

Feast dates: the Church’s own dates are used (25 September for the repose, 5 July for the finding of the relics, both Julian), with the civil dates (8 October, 18 July) given in the biography. The feast_day_orthodox field holds 25 September. Other drafts are not consistent on Julian or civil dates, so the owner may want to set one rule.
